summary.text: Writing $m=(p-1)/2$ and $C=m!$, Euler’s criterion and a binomial/Vandermonde factorization show that the relevant power matrix is nonsingular whenever $D^mC\ne1$; the half-Wilson congruence $C^2=(-1)^{m+1}$ supplies this for $D=C$ when $p\equiv1\pmod4$, and for the auxiliary choice $D=-C$ when $p\equiv3\pmod4$. In the latter case $C=\pm1$, and the quadratic-character correlation $\sum_t\chi(x_i-t)\chi(x_j+t)=1$, split into the two signed half-intervals, gives $AB^T+BA^T=0$ for the target matrix $A$ and the invertible auxiliary matrix $B$; since $m$ is odd, taking determinants forces $\det A=0$.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_n\) denote the \(n\)-th prime, with \(p_1=2,p_2=3,\ldots\). Fix \(n\ge 2\), put
\[
p=p_n,\qquad m=\frac{p-1}{2},\qquad C=m!,
\]
and define the integer matrix
\[
A=(A_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le m},\qquad
A_{ij}=\left(\frac{i^2-Cj}{p}\right).
\]
Here \((\frac{\cdot}{p})\) is the Legendre symbol. Since \(n\ge2\), the prime \(p\) is odd and \(p\ge3\). By definition, \(a(n)=\det A\). We prove
\[
\det A=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\equiv3\pmod4.
\]

Throughout the proof, reductions modulo \(p\) are regarded as elements of the field \(\mathbb F_p\). We use the same letter \(C\) for the residue of \(m!\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). This element is nonzero because \(m<p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The half-Wilson identity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We first record the identity
\[
C^2=(-1)^{m+1}\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, since \(p=2m+1\), split Wilson's product into its lower and upper halves. The upper-half elements \(m+1,\ldots,2m\), in reverse order, are
\[
2m,2m-1,\ldots,m+1,
\]
and modulo \(p=2m+1\) these are
\[
-1,-2,\ldots,-m.
\]
Consequently
\[
(p-1)!=(2m)!\equiv (1\cdot2\cdots m)((-1)(-2)\cdots(-m))
=(-1)^m(m!)^2=(-1)^m C^2\pmod p.
\]
Wilson's theorem says \((p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p\). Multiplying by \((-1)^m\) gives (1).

Two consequences will be needed.

* If \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), then \(m\) is even, so \(m+1\) is odd and (1) gives
  \[
  C^2=-1. \tag{2}
  \]

* If \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), then \(m\) is odd, so \(m+1\) is even and (1) gives
  \[
  C^2=1. \tag{3}
  \]
  Since \(\mathbb F_p\) is a field, (3) implies
  \[
  C=1\quad\text{or}\quad C=-1. \tag{4}
  \]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. A finite-field determinant criterion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We next establish the nonvanishing criterion used twice below.

Let \(D\in\mathbb F_p^\times\), and for \(1\le i,j\le m\) set
\[
x_i=i^2,\qquad b_j=Dj.
\]
Consider the matrix
\[
L_D=\bigl((x_i-b_j)^m\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m}. \tag{5}
\]
We claim that
\[
D^m C\ne1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \det L_D\ne0. \tag{6}
\]

We prove this by an explicit factorization. First, the elements \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) are pairwise distinct in \(\mathbb F_p\). For if \(i^2=j^2\), then
\[
(i-j)(i+j)=0.
\]
Thus either \(i=j\), or \(i+j=0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). The second alternative is impossible because \(2\le i+j\le2m=p-1\). Hence the Vandermonde matrix
\[
V_x=(x_i^k)_{\substack{1\le i\le m\\0\le k<m}}
\]
has nonzero determinant.

Likewise the \(b_j\)'s are nonzero and pairwise distinct because \(D\ne0\) and \(1,\ldots,m\) are distinct nonzero residues. Put
\[
z_j=(-b_j)^{-1}.
\]
Then the \(z_j\)'s are pairwise distinct.

Define an \(m\times m\) matrix \(E\), with rows indexed by \(k=0,\ldots,m-1\), by
\[
E_{0j}=1+z_j^m,
\qquad
E_{kj}=z_j^k\quad(1\le k<m). \tag{7}
\]
Its determinant has the closed form
\[
\det E=
\left(1-(-1)^m\prod_{j=1}^m z_j\right)
\prod_{1\le r<s\le m}(z_s-z_r). \tag{8}
\]
To see this, transpose \(E\). It is the ordinary Vandermonde matrix in the \(z_j\)'s, except that its constant column has been replaced by the sum of the constant column and the column \((z_j^m)_j\). By linearity of the determinant in that column, its determinant is the sum of the ordinary Vandermonde determinant and the determinant obtained by replacing the constant column with \((z_j^m)_j\). Move this new highest-power column from the first position to the last; this contributes \((-1)^{m-1}\). After factoring \(z_j\) from row \(j\), what remains is again the ordinary Vandermonde matrix. Thus the second contribution is
\[
(-1)^{m-1}\left(\prod_jz_j\right)\det(V_z),
\]
which gives (8).

Now
\[
\prod_{j=1}^m z_j
=\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(-b_j)\right)^{-1}
=\left((-1)^m\prod_{j=1}^m b_j\right)^{-1}.
\]
Therefore the first factor in (8) is nonzero exactly when \(\prod_jb_j\ne1\). Since the \(z_j\)'s are distinct, the Vandermonde factor is nonzero. Hence
\[
\prod_jb_j\ne1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \det E\ne0. \tag{9}
\]
But
\[
\prod_{j=1}^m b_j
=\prod_{j=1}^m(Dj)=D^m m!=D^mC. \tag{10}
\]

It remains to connect \(E\) to \(L_D\). Let
\[
c_0=1,
\qquad c_k=\binom mk\quad(1\le k<m).
\]
Every \(c_k\) is nonzero in \(\mathbb F_p\): all factorials occurring in \(\binom mk=m!/(k!(m-k)!)\) involve integers strictly below \(p\). Also, Fermat's theorem gives
\[
x_i^m=(i^2)^m=i^{p-1}=1. \tag{11}
\]
Using \(y=-b_j\), the binomial expansion can be written with its final term folded into the \(k=0\) term:
\[
(x_i+y)^m
=
\left((1+y^{-m})y^m\right)
+
\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}x_i^k\binom mk y^{m-k}. \tag{12}
\]
Indeed, the first displayed term is \(y^m+1\), and the \(1\) is the omitted \(k=m\) binomial term \(x_i^m\), by (11). Since \(z_j=y^{-1}\), equation (12) yields the matrix factorization
\[
L_D
=V_x\,\operatorname{diag}(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})\,
E\,\operatorname{diag}\bigl((-b_1)^m,\ldots,(-b_m)^m\bigr). \tag{13}
\]
Every factor on the right has nonzero determinant if \(D^mC\ne1\): this follows respectively from the distinctness of the \(x_i\)'s, the nonvanishing of the binomial coefficients, (9) and (10), and the nonvanishing of every \(b_j\). This proves (6).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Nonvanishing when \(p\equiv1\pmod4\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume \(p\equiv1\pmod4\). Then \(m\) is even and (2) says \(C^2=-1\). We show
\[
C^{m+1}\ne1. \tag{14}
\]
If it were equal to \(1\), then its square would be \(1\). On the other hand,
\[
(C^{m+1})^2=(C^2)^{m+1}=(-1)^{m+1}=-1,
\]
because \(m+1\) is odd. This would imply \(1=-1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), impossible for the odd prime \(p\).

Apply criterion (6) with \(D=C\). Its required product is
\[
D^mC=C^{m+1},
\]
which is not \(1\) by (14). Thus
\[
\det\bigl((i^2-Cj)^m\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m}\ne0
\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p. \tag{15}
\]

Euler's criterion identifies this matrix with the reduction modulo \(p\) of the original Legendre-symbol matrix. More precisely, for every integer \(u\), the residue in \(\mathbb F_p\) of \((\frac up)\in\{-1,0,1\}\) equals \(u^{(p-1)/2}=u^m\). Hence the reduction modulo \(p\) of \(A\) is exactly the matrix in (15). Determinants commute with reduction modulo \(p\), so (15) says that the integer \(\det A\) has nonzero residue modulo \(p\). In particular,
\[
p\equiv1\pmod4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\det A\ne0. \tag{16}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. A nonzero auxiliary determinant when \(p\equiv3\pmod4\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Now assume \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). Thus \(m\) is odd and \(C^2=1\). Introduce the auxiliary integer matrix
\[
B=(B_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le m},
\qquad
B_{ij}=\left(\frac{i^2+Cj}{p}\right).
\]
This is the same construction with the factorial coefficient \(C\) replaced by \(-C\).

Apply criterion (6) with \(D=-C\). Since \(m\) is odd and \(m+1\) is even,
\[
(-C)^mC=-C^{m+1}=-1,
\]
where \(C^{m+1}=1\) follows from \(C^2=1\). Because \(p\) is odd, \(-1\ne1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). Therefore
\[
\det\bigl((i^2+Cj)^m\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m}\ne0
\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.
\]
By Euler's criterion this is the reduction of \(B\), and hence
\[
\det B\ne0\quad\text{as an integer}. \tag{17}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. The quadratic-character sum
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(\chi:\mathbb F_p\to\{-1,0,1\}\) be the quadratic character, with \(\chi(0)=0\). For \(p\equiv3\pmod4\),
\[
\chi(-1)=-1. \tag{18}
\]
This is Euler's criterion: \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}=(-1)^m=-1\).

We need the following character-sum identity. If \(a+b\ne0\), then
\[
\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p}\chi(a-t)\chi(b+t)=-\chi(-1). \tag{19}
\]
For completeness, let \(s=a+b\ne0\), and make the bijective substitution
\[
a-t=su,\qquad b+t=s(1-u).
\]
Since \(\chi(s)^2=1\), the sum becomes
\[
\sum_{u\in\mathbb F_p}\chi(u)\chi(1-u)
=\sum_u\chi(u(1-u)). \tag{20}
\]
We evaluate this last sum directly. First,
\[
\chi(u(1-u))=\chi(-1)\chi(u^2-u).
\]
The number \(N\) of pairs \((u,y)\in\mathbb F_p^2\) satisfying
\[
y^2=u^2-u
\]
is
\[
N=\sum_u\bigl(1+\chi(u^2-u)\bigr)
=p+\sum_u\chi(u^2-u). \tag{21}
\]
Because \(2\) is invertible, the equation may be rewritten by setting \(v=2u-1\) and \(w=2y\):
\[
v^2-w^2=1,
\qquad (v-w)(v+w)=1.
\]
Its solutions correspond bijectively to choices of \(q=v-w\in\mathbb F_p^\times\): then \(v+w=q^{-1}\), and \(v,w\), hence \(u,y\), are uniquely determined. Thus \(N=p-1\). Comparing with (21) gives
\[
\sum_u\chi(u^2-u)=-1.
\]
Substitution into (20) proves (19).

For our application set
\[
x_i=i^2\in\mathbb F_p,\qquad 1\le i\le m.
\]
For every \(i,j\),
\[
x_i+x_j\ne0. \tag{22}
\]
Indeed, if \(i^2+j^2=0\), then, since \(j\ne0\),
\[
(ij^{-1})^2=-1,
\]
contradicting (18), which says that \(-1\) is not a square.

Applying (19) to \(a=x_i,b=x_j\), and using (18), gives
\[
\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p}\chi(x_i-t)\chi(x_j+t)=1. \tag{23}
\]
The nonzero elements of \(\mathbb F_p\) are precisely
\[
1,2,\ldots,m,-1,-2,\ldots,-m.
\]
The term of (23) at \(t=0\) is
\[
\chi(x_i)\chi(x_j)=1,
\]
because each \(x_i\) is a nonzero square. Removing that term and partitioning the remaining residues into the two displayed halves yields
\[
\sum_{k=1}^m\chi(x_i-k)\chi(x_j+k)
+
\sum_{k=1}^m\chi(x_i+k)\chi(x_j-k)=0. \tag{24}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The skew product relation and vanishing
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Regard the integer matrices \(A,B\) as rational matrices. Their entries can be written
\[
A_{ik}=\chi(x_i-Ck),
\qquad
B_{ik}=\chi(x_i+Ck). \tag{25}
\]
Recall from (4) that \(C=1\) or \(C=-1\).

If \(C=1\), the \((i,j)\)-entry of
\[
AB^{T}+BA^{T}
\]
is exactly the left side of (24), and is therefore zero. If \(C=-1\), the two sums are merely interchanged, so the same conclusion holds. Thus
\[
AB^{T}+BA^{T}=0. \tag{26}
\]

We now use that the matrix size \(m\) is odd. From (26),
\[
AB^{T}=-BA^{T}.
\]
Taking determinants over \(\mathbb Q\), and using \(\det(M^T)=\det M\), gives
\[
\det A\det B
=\det(-BA^T)
=(-1)^m\det B\det A
=-\det A\det B.
\]
Therefore
\[
2\det A\det B=0.
\]
The field \(\mathbb Q\) has characteristic zero, and \(\det B\ne0\) by (17). Hence \(\det A=0\) in \(\mathbb Q\), and therefore also as an integer. We have proved
\[
p\equiv3\pmod4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\det A=0. \tag{27}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Completion and the sequence indexing
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Every odd prime is congruent to either \(1\) or \(3\) modulo \(4\). For our \(p=p_n\) with \(n\ge2\), implication (16) excludes vanishing in the \(1\pmod4\) case, while (27) proves vanishing in the \(3\pmod4\) case. Thus
\[
a(n)=\det A=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p_n\equiv3\pmod4.
\]
This includes \(n=2\), where \(p_2=3\), \(m=1\), \(C=1\), and the sole matrix entry is \((\frac{1-1}{3})=0\). Hence the claimed equivalence holds for every \(n\ge2\).
